newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-BROOKS NOT WORRIED ABOUT ELS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-BROOKS NOT WORRIED ABOUT ELS.

text.p: Mark Brooks seemed unworried on Friday about the prospect of playing holder Ernie Els in the World Matchplay semifinals on Saturday.
The U.S. PGA champion may be only five feet nine (1.75 metres) and weigh just 67 kgs, but Brooks feels he can be a match for anyone, even the imposing South African who has never lost in this event.

"If I can get out of the blocks quickly and play the first four or five holes well, I can give anyone a match," the 35-year-old Texan said after disposing of European number one Colin Montgomerie by one hole on Friday.
"I've got to be the underdog, against anybody. I'm the smallest and the shortest hitter. But we'll see."
He is finding the 6,957-yard West Course at Wentworth a test of his patience as it is playing every yard of its length and more after heavy rain on Friday morning and again in the evening.
"If the course were playing fast, I would like my chances better. I would prefer firmer conditions, like it is when they play the British PGA here in the spring," he said.
Els, chasing a third successive title which no one has achieved here, had a great escape from six holes down to Steve Stricker on Friday.
The morning round belonged to the 29-year-old American, who won all five of his Alfred Dunhill Cup matches last week before beating Steve Elkington of Australia in the first round here.
He made six birdies, to one for the South African. But Els responded like a true champion with eight birdies including two chip-ins in the afternoon.
Els won at the last with a three-foot birdie putt that just dropped into the hole through the side door.
"This is a great feeling but I felt for Steve," said Els, the top seed. "To come to the last hole and lose after leading all day, I felt for him."

Unseeded Fijian Vijay Singh made another strong start and accounted for his second seed in two days, following his opening day win over Phil Mickelson with a 9 and 8 thrashing of U.S. Open champion Steve Jones, the third seed.
Singh made only two bogeys all day, both in the morning. "If he was going to beat me, he had to make birdies," Singh said.
Powerful British Open champion Tom Lehman seized control early against fellow American Mark O'Meara and motored impressively to a 6 and 5 victory.
Seven birdies in the 13 holes the afternoon round gave Lehman a runaway triumph and a semifinal encounter with Singh, who also reached the last four two years ago.
